author: Ivan Goncharov
introFa: کتاب «Oblomov» نوشته Ivan Goncharov یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Oblomov»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Haloperidol and Limb Deformity To the Editor.\p=m-\Thecontinuing possi- bility that a potent new teratogen will come into general use in the guise of a safe and effective drug has prompted us to view with concern all reports of drug-associated malforma- tions. Last winter we learned of the case reported in this issue of The Journal (p 62) of a child born with limb-reduction deformities, whose mother had taken haloperidol and other drugs early in pregnancy. In an attempt to clarify any possible rela- tionship between this drug and other cases of reduction deformities, we reviewed the prenatal drug-exposure histories of children with similar de- fects born in Metropolitan Atlanta in the past four years. Haloperidol has been used in the treatment of a variety of psychoses and psychotic reactions in Europe since 1958 and in the United States since 1967. Little information on the teratogenic potential of haloperidol is available from the literature. Experi- ments in several different species of mammals have given contradictory re- sults. Studies on the use of haloperi¬ dol in the -treatment of hyperemesis gravidarum have not shown a con¬ sistently higher malformation rate for exposed fetuses than for con¬ trols.12 Drug dosages in these studies were lower than psychotherapeutic dosages, however, and the numbers of exposed women were relatively small. Furthermore, defects were not ade¬ quately defined and categorized to permit evaluation of individual ab¬ normalities. One case report1 noted the occurrence of reduction defor¬ mities in the infant of a woman treated with haloperidol and other drugs while her fetus was in the limb- sensitive organogenetic period of ges¬ tation as defined by the thalidomide experience. We concluded from this that a teratogenic potential for halo¬ peridol had not been completely ex¬ cluded. The files of the Metropolitan At¬ lanta Congenital Defects Program' include reports on 86 infants with limb-reduction deformities born be¬ tween Jan 1, 1970, and Oct 31, 1973. We reviewed these case reports and selected families of the 38 infants with the most severe reduction defor¬ mities for interview. Minor degrees of deformity or those for which a ge¬ netic etiology was suspected were ex¬ cluded. Each of the 31 mothers inter- viewed was shown a sample of the dosage forms of haloperidol marketed in this country and asked if she re¬ called having taken this drug at any time in her pregnancy. Responses were not corroborated. No mother recalled having taken this drug while pregnant, although one reported having taken it subse¬ quently. Hospital records of the seven women we did not interview gave no evidence of exposure to this drug. Pri¬ vate obstetrician records of three of these women showed no haloperidol prescriptions. Thus we found no evi¬ dence of an association between halo¬ peridol usage during pregnancy and limb-reduction deformities in these cases. The results of this study do not sup¬ port the hypothesis that haloperidol causes reduction deformities. How¬ ever, findings from a small study based on parental recall, such as this one, should be interpreted with cau¬ tion. Nevertheless, it seems unlikely that haloperidol has caused any se¬ vere reduction deformities in Atlanta during the period of 1970 to 1973. James W. Hanson, MD Godfrey P. New York, Academic Press, Inc, 1971, pp 155-158. "Oblomov Syndrome"? ("Oblomov Sign"?) To the Editor.\p=m-\Iwas particularly interested in the statement of N. S. Kline, MD, that refusal to get out of bed may be one of symptoms of de- pression (227:1158, 1974). Taking into consideration the ex- isting tendency to seek literary ar- chetypes for various clinical syn- dromes, eg, Pickwickian syndrome, Munchausen syndrome, Ondine syn- drome, Musset syndrome, I would like to note that the refusal to get out of bed also has a representative in belles lettres. It's Ilya Ilych Oblomov, lead- ing character of Oblomov, a novel written in 1859 by the Russian classic author, Ivan Gentcharov (1812-1891). Through 131 pages (one third of the book!), Oblomov, a 32-year-old noble- man, refuses to get out of bed. Throughout many hours he tries to overcome his passivity but without result. This part of the book is deeply disturbing. After many sad events, over a couple of years, Oblomov dies of cerebral hemorrhage. Taking all this into consideration, may I propose for patients who refuse to get out of bed a new syndrome, Ob¬ lomov syndrome? Wladyslaw Wermut, MD Gdynia-Redlowe, Poland Instead of Oblomov "syndrome," perhaps Oblomov "sign"? Or even Oblomov "symp- tom"?)-ED. Gastric Phytobezoar To the Editor.\p=m-\Theuse of endoscopy in the dissolution of gastric phytobe- zoar (229:1332, 1974) is elegant, but perhaps should be reserved until oral- ly administered enzymes have been tried. The efficacy of cellulase in dis- solving phytobezoar was reported by Pollard and Block1 and confirmed by Deal et al.2 I encountered a case of phytobezoar in a 56-year-old man with subtotal gastrectomy (Billroth I) nine months following vagectomy for marginal ul- cer. His history included ingestion of three oranges per day for several months. On the basis of Pollard's protocol, the patient was given a five\x=req-\ day course of three pulverized Gastro- enterase tablets (containing pepsin, pancreatic enzyme concentrate, cellu- lase, and dehydrocholic acid) after each meal, which he took as an out- patient. An upper gastrointestinal roentgenographic series immediately thereafter showed complete disap- pearance of the bezoar. This case supports the use of oral- ly administered chemicals for bezoar and recommends it as a noninvasive, simple first step in the treatment of the entity. The agent to be used de¬ pends on patient history and geogra¬ phy.3 Proper education of the patient with a partial gastrectomy, partic¬ ularly if a vagotomy has also been performed, should decrease the inci¬ dence of this postgastrectomy syn¬ drome.4 Harold M.
